McDonald and Goggins were arrested by military police and charged with leaving their posts without orders. Their sergeant, Joseph Stones, was charged with "shamefully casting away his arms" after jamming his rifle across a trench to slow down the enemy rush. They were tried at a court martial on Christmas Eve 1916. Despite testimonies from other officers stating McDonald was a brave soldier who was not capable of cowardice, they were found guilty. Brigadier-General H. O'Donnell and Field Marshal Douglas Haig confirmed the death sentences, stating the executions were necessary to "set an example" to a shaken battalion. At 7:36 AM on 18 January 1917, McDonald, Goggins, and Stones were blindfolded, tied to stakes, and executed by a British firing squad in Rouellecourt, France. McDonald was 28 years old

Private Ernest Mackness was a British soldier who was executed by firing squad for desertion on 1 October 1917 during the First World War. He is laid to rest on the north side of the Blaringhem Churchyard in the Nord department of France. Despite his execution, historical military records show his father was granted a war gratuity on 2 April 1918.

Sapper Frederick Malyon of 12 Company Royal Engineers. It is known that at the time of his offence he was attached to the Royal Field Artillery, and his army number would suggest that he was well above the average age of those executed for military offences. No details have been discovered about his desertion, the only further information being that he was shot at Noeux-les-Mines on 4 April. On the day that America joined the war

Lance Corporal Allassan Mamprusi was a soldier in the Gold Coast Regiment of the West African Frontier Force (WAFF) who was executed by firing squad for cowardice during World War I. Part of the Gold Coast Regiment, West African Frontier Force. While Mamprusi's unit had been successfully engaging and ambushing German colonial patrols in East Africa, he found the intense psychological stress of combat overwhelming and was accused of cowardice. Following a court-martial, Mamprusi was sentenced to death and executed just three days after his trial. Because he was "Shot at Dawn" by military execution, his name is included on historical lists of World War I colonial troops executed under British military authority. He is commemorated alongside other fallen soldiers on the Kumasi Memorial in Ghana

He enlisted in Sept 1914, under the name of Harris & went to France in May 1915.  He was initially enthusiastic, but disenchantment set in after his first spell of front-line duty. Just before Christmas, at Givenchy, Harris was wounded in the back by the explosion of a German mine, but returned to his unit from hospital on 19 Jan. On the morning of 13 Feb, at Sailly la Bourse, Harris reported to a senior NCO, saying that he had been sent from the trenches suffering from the shock from a rifle-grenade; that he had failed to find a dressing-station the previous night; & that he had spent the night at Vermelles.  He was taken to see a doctor, who however   said that Harris was fit for duty.  (The doctor in question was to say at trial that Harris complained of deafness; but that he had found him to be suffering from no appreciable disease, or from nerves). Harris was sent with a note, & ordered to report to the Adjutant in the trenches; went off at about 1000-1030 in that direction, but made no such report. On 13 Feb, at about 1100, Harris was seen by a Corporal at the farm where he was billeted, saying that he had just come out of hospital.  Later that day, he was arrested when he finally said that his regiment was in the trenches.  His French landlady said that Harris had arrived between 1500 & 1600, telling her that ‘….the Germans had been bombing our trenches & he had left them & was going to England’. At trial, Harris testified, saying: ‘I left the trenches because 3 rifle-grenades exploded near me. I was deafened & my nerves had gone a bit’. When ordered back to the trenches, he had felt nervous  & lost his head, ending up at his billet, thinking to return to duty after a few days.  Under cross-examination, however he admitted his intention not to return until the company came out of the trenches. Following conviction, his good character was proved, but in vain. Private Harry Martin, 9th Bn. Essex Regiment, executed for desertion 20th March 1916.

Private James Mayers (Service Number 492050) was a British soldier executed for desertion during World War I on 16 June 1917. He served in the 1st/13th (Kensington) Battalion of the London Regiment. He was one of the 306 British and Commonwealth soldiers "shot at dawn" for military disciplinary offences, most of whom were posthumously pardoned by the British Ministry of Defence in 2006. He was the son of Mrs M. E. Mayers and lived at 193 Morning Lane, Hackney, London. Mayers arrived on the Western Front in France in September 1916 as part of the replacements sent to cover heavy losses from the Battle of the Somme. Before the incident that led to his death, he had already received a death sentence for quitting his post, which the military high command had commuted to a suspended sentence so he could be sent back to the front lines. After a subsequent desertion, his suspended sentence was enacted. He was executed by firing squad at the age of 25. His remains are located at the Achicourt Road Cemetery near Pas-de-Calais, France,

Rifleman Samuel McBride was a British soldier executed for desertion during World War I. He was shot by a firing squad in the pre-dawn darkness on 7 December 1916 at Hope Farm, located near Ploegsteert Wood in Belgium. McBride served with the 2nd Battalion, Royal Irish Rifles. After enduring heavy fighting and intense German artillery shelling, he went missing from his unit for four months. At his court-martial, McBride lacked legal representation. He defended himself by stating he was exhausted, suffering from severe headaches, and sore all over. Two sergeants from his battalion testified in his support, noting he had a history of volunteering for dangerous tasks. The military authorities chose to make an example of him to deter other soldiers from abandoning their duties, ignoring his clear medical distress. Modern assessments by historians and government officials indicate his symptoms closely matched what is now recognized as shell shock(Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder). He is buried at the Hyde Park Corner (Royal Berks) Cemetery in Comines-Warneton, Hainaut, Belgium

Private Harry McClair and Private Frederick Johnson had enlisted together in the Border Regiment. Towards the end of 1915 the two men had been posted to 2 Battalion on the Western Front.72 The date when they absconded is not known, but when they were arrested in the summer of 1918, they must have been absent for some considerable time, because their division (the 7th) had been transferred to Italy at the end of 1917. Between their trial and confirmation of their sentences, the two middle-aged Scots were held at Caserne Pepinière in Paris. On 31 July they were enjoying a boisterous game of football with other soldiers when they were informed by a cavalry officer that they would be executed on the following day. By arrangement with the French authorities, the pair were transferred to Vincennes, where the former had already executed 27 spies and traitors.

Private Charles Frederick McColl (Service No. 11/81) of the 1/4th Battalion, East Yorkshire Regiment, was executed by a British Army firing squad for desertion on 28 December 1917 at the age of 26. He joined the 11th East Yorkshire Regiment in 1914, serving in Egypt before being deployed to the Western Front. In September 1916, near Neuve Chapelle, McColl was buried by an exploding shell. He was invalided back to the UK suffering from severe trauma, officially noted as "heart failure and nervousness" (what is today recognized as Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder or shell shock). He was sent back to France without receiving a medical clearance examination and was re-assigned to the 1/4th Battalion.  McColl struggled significantly upon his return to active duty, leading to a succession of disciplinary issues. He went absent without leave, was caught in Étaples, and received a suspended 10-year prison sentence on the condition he return to the front. He absconded again, was caught three miles behind the lines, and was sentenced to 90 days of Field Punishment No. 1. On 28 October, during the brutal Third Battle of Ypres (Passchendaele), McColl abandoned his weapon and equipment in the support trenches near Houlthulst Forest. He fled to Calais, where he was arrested on 1 November after attempting to sneak into a rest camp to return to England.  During his court-martial, McColl pleaded "not guilty". He was not represented by legal counsel. He explained to the panel that his nervous condition made it impossible to control himself while under fire in the trenches. No medical examination was ordered to review his mental health, and he was sentenced to death. He was held at Brandhoek before being moved to Ypres, where he was informed his death sentence was confirmed. At dawn on 28 December 1917, he was strapped to a chair in front of a 10-man firing squad made up of soldiers from his own platoon. Five men were given live ammunition and five were given blanks so no individual would definitively know who fired the lethal shot. Following his execution, McColl’s military medals were forfeited and his family was denied a war pension. He was buried in the Ypres Reservoir Cemetery in Belgium

On 27 February the trials of two soldiers from the same battalion, 15 Royal Irish Rifles took place. It is significant that one of the men, who had a history of previous convictions, was unrepresented at his trial. Rifleman McCracken and Rifleman Templeton both came from Belfast and had served with the battalion since it arrived in France the previous October. McCracken, who was aged 19 years, and Templeton were both tried for desertion, the only military offence for which soldiers were executed during the first quarter of 1916. The court heard that McCracken had three previous convictions, two involving absence. The duo were executed side-by-side on 19 March and were buried at Mailly-Maillet.

Unit: 17th Battalion Notts and Derby's Regiment (Sherwood Foresters)
Notes: Private Bertie McCubbin was a British soldier who was executed by firing squad for military offences during the First World War. He was executed at dawn on 30 July 1916 at the age of 22. McCubbin served in the 17th Battalion, Sherwood Foresters (Nottinghamshire and Derbyshire Regiment). He volunteered early in the war and had been serving in the frontline trenches for four months by July 1916. On 7 July 1916, while stationed near Aubers Ridge, McCubbin refused an order to go into No Man’s Land to occupy a listening post. He was charged with "misbehaviour before the enemy in such a way as to show cowardice" and "wilful defiance" for disobeying an officer. McCubbin stated that a recent close-range shell burst had ruined his nerves. He argued his refusal was due to extreme nervousness from continuous bombardment rather than blank defiance, stating, "If I go over, I shall be a danger to the other man who is out there as well as to myself." His Adjutant gave evidence that McCubbin had previously performed his duties well, but note that over the last six months he had become "unstrung" after spending 26 consecutive days in the trenches. Despite recommendations for mercy due to his psychological state, the death sentence was upheld. He was executed alongside fellow battalion member George Lowton. He is buried at the Brown's Road Military Cemetery in Festubert, France

Private John McFarlane (Service Number 265427) was a British soldier who was executed by firing squad for desertion during the First World War. He served with the 4th Battalion of The King's (Liverpool Regiment). Military research records show he was officially reported as suffering from shell-shock in November 1916 (under his earlier four-digit service number, 2070) and was later wounded in action in September 1917. He was shot at dawn on 22 May 1918 at the age of 27. He is buried at the Nine Elms British Cemetery in Poperinge, West-Vlaanderen, Belgium

Private Bernard McGeehan was a World War I soldier who was executed by the British Army for desertion on 2 November 1916. In 2006, 90 years after his death, he was granted a posthumous military pardon by the British government as part of a collective pardon for 306 executed soldiers. Born in Raphoe, County Donegal, Ireland, in 1888, his family later relocated to Derry. He worked in the Post Office in Derry. He volunteered for the British Army in 1914 following the outbreak of the war. He served as a Private (Service Number 2974) in the 1/8th Battalion, The King’s (Liverpool Regiment).  After serving 18 months on the Western Front without any leave, McGeehan suffered a severe psychological breakdown, commonly referred to then as "shell shock" (now recognized as PTSD). He walked out of his trench line on 19 September 1916. Five days later, he voluntarily approached military lines looking for food and water and trying to find his regiment. His court-martial lasted minutes and was preserved on just two pages of handwritten notes. In his own defence, McGeehan stated that fellow soldiers had constantly bullied and thrown stones at him, and that he did not know what he was doing when he wandered away. The military judges dismissed his shattered mental state, declaring him of "weak intellect" and "worthless as a soldier". He was sentenced to death to serve as a disciplinary example to others. McGeehan was executed by a British firing squad at 6:16 AM on 2 November 1916. He was 28 years old. He is buried at the Poperinghe New Military Cemetery in Belgium

Private John McQuade was a British Army soldier executed by firing squad for desertion on 6 November 1916 during World War I. He was one of the 306 British and Commonwealth soldiers "shot at dawn" who received a posthumous royal pardon from the British government in 2006. Served in 18th Battalion, Highland Light Infantry (HLI). During the Battle of the Somme, McQuade was attached to the 106th Trench Mortar Battery as a shell/bomb carrier. On 29 July 1916, he was ordered to move to the trenches but was missing when the battery assembled. He had previously dropped out of a marching column citing exhaustion. He was apprehended in Corbie and returned to his battalion on 15 August 1916. Military authorities took a harsh stance because McQuade already had a prior conviction for disobedience, which carried a suspended sentence of one year's imprisonment. He was tried by a Field General Court Martial, sentenced to death, and shot at dawn on 6 November 1916

Private James Michael was a volunteer serving in 10 Cameronians (Scottish Rifles), and his death came just ten weeks after that of another deserter from the same battalion. Early in the summer of 1917 Michael’s comrades had taken part in the fighting in the Salient, whilst the reluctant soldier had made off. The inevitable execution was recorded in the unit’s history, the diarist noting that it was the second case in the battalion. Private Michael was shot at Poperinghe, becoming the twelfth victim to die in front of the firing squads in this Belgian town immediately behind the Ypres Salient. Like the previously executed deserter from the battalion Michael was commemorated in post-war years in the regiment’s casualty roll. Both victims were natives of Glasgow and by chance the two names appear on the same page of this official record. No cause of death is recorded for either soldier.

Private John Milburn had enlisted for service in the Northumberland Fusiliers and served in France with a Tyneside Irish battalion – which was ultimately amalgamated to form 24/27 Northumberland Fusiliers. Milburn was serving under a suspended sentence of 2 years’ imprisonment when he deserted in order to avoid serving in the trenches opposite the Hindenburg Line. He was executed by firing squad for desertion during World War I on 8 November 1917

Private Charles Milligan had enlisted in February 1916 into the Cameronians (Scottish Rifles). Once in France the soldier had committed his first offence of disobedience in October of the same year. The resultant sentence of one year’s imprisonment with hard labour was obviously suspended, as early in 1917 the private was again convicted for the same offence – but on this occasion received the more lenient sentence of 42 days’ field punishment no.1. The young soldier’s battalion was part of 15 (Scottish) Division and was engaged in the opening day of the Battle of Arras, as well as on a number of days thereafter. And it was at this time that Private Milligan went absent – just as his unit was preparing to attack. The soldier’s freedom was short-lived, and five days later he was arrested. A court martial disposed of Milligan’s case on 5 May when once again a soldier with a bad record chose to be unrepresented. The Scotsman’s unfortunate admissions included one that, at the moment he fled, he had been unable to control his actions. His commanding officer, Lieutenant-Colonel A C Stanley-Clarke, was very fairminded in his written statement to the court. He recorded that Milligan’s conduct ‘has not been good on the whole’, although there is ‘nothing to his discredit in the field’.86 The brigade commander however, was not so charitable about the 20 year old. He recommended that the sentence be carried out, adding that men even younger had been known to do their duty in the past.87 Private Milligan’s death on 3 June 1917 was later recorded in the official casualty rolls, but no cause of death was stated.88 Although the Glaswegian received such commemoration, in post-war years the Imperial War Graves Commission were unable to locate his grave. But in later years the diligent staff of the Commission did identify his remains, which today lie in Canadian Cemetery No.2 at Neuville St Vaast – near Arras. Rather strangely, and by way of an oversight, Private Milligan had initially been commemorated on the Menin Gate Memorial to the Missing. In fact the correct location would have been on the Arras Memorial.

Unit: 2nd Battalion Duke of Cornwall's Light Infantry
Notes: George Mills, the son of Mrs Pilling of 142 Mortlake Road, was born in East London in 1894. George volunteered for enlistment into the Duke of Cornwall’s Light Infantry on the 24th February 1915. Little is known of his background except that he was born in the East End of London in 1894, and is alleged (but not officially recorded) to have had a police record at the time of his enlistment. Within a matter of a couple of weeks, on the 15th of March 1915 he crossed to France in a troopship, and reported to the 2nd Battalion DCLI later the same day. The date indicates that he could not have completed more than a fortnight’s training, however the recruit training programme of the time was designed to last for six months. This period was occasionally shortened when the manpower demand on the western front was critical. It was, however, unprecedented for this to occur. His arrival coincided with the 2nd Battalion which was resting out of the line in billets at the Rue de Lettre about two miles south of Erquingham near Armentieres. He was initially employed as a company orderly and later as the soldier-servant of Lieutenant Evelyn Mulock. When the Battalion went up into the line again, Mills was, for some reason, left behind in billets with the rear details. On 31st July 1915, he stole money, documents and general property belonging to Lieutenant Mulock, 2nd Lieutenant Martin and Private Lucas. Then, dressing himself in officer’s uniform, he went to Boulogne to enjoy his stolen goods. He was quickly arrested. A field general court Martial was held at Boulogne on 10th September 1915. Mills conducted his own defence; it is not recorded whether he was accorded his legal right to be represented by a defending officer, or whether he refused to exercise that right. In his defence he stated: “ The other officers’ servants were always drinking and wanting to fight one another… The other servants were down on me because I did not drink. I dressed as an officer so as not to be stopped by the sentry of my regiment… I intended to go home for a few days and come back again. ” He was shot at 5:03 a.m by a firing squad on 29th September 1915.

Private Arthur Mitchell had landed at Helles on the Gallipoli peninsula on 5 May 1915.9 His battalion, 1/6 Lancashire Fusiliers, was one of four Fusilier units from Lancashire which had landed simultaneously. The battalions were all part of 42 Division, and did not arrive on the Western Front until March 1917. Evidence given at Mitchell’s trial stated that the private had gone absent prior to a tour of duty in the trenches. He had then been arrested nine days later when working in a field. The soldier had discarded his uniform and was wearing blue trousers and a French police bonnet! Whilst perhaps it did not substantially detract from the conspicuous nature of the absentee’s chosen headgear, the court did hear that the private had shaved off his moustache. The unfortunate soldier, who like so many, had endured hell on earth at Gallipoli, was executed at Achiet-le-Grand, mid-way between the Somme and Arras fronts. In the third week of August a sixth soldier was shot from the 15 (Scottish) Division.

Private Leonard Mitchell had served in 1/5 Yorks & Lancs – part of 49 (West Riding) Division – before being posted to the 8th battalion of this regiment. The soldier had an unenviable reputation to live down, being under a suspended sentence of death for an offence of desertion. However, Private Mitchell did not conform, and decamped from the Ypres Salient when the dangers of active service became too great for his constitution. His execution took place in the small village of La Clytte, some distance away from the front. On the day that the Battle of the Menin Road Ridge commenced a very young colonial soldier was shot. It was over two years since a soldier as young as 17 had been lined-up before a firing squad, and again the victim had seen only brief service.

Private Thomas Lionel Moles was a Canadian infantryman who was executed by firing squad for desertion during the First World War. He was shot at dawn at 05:50 am on 22 October 1917 at Ypres Prison in Belgium. He served with the 54th Canadian Infantry Battalion (Central Ontario Regiment) of the Canadian Expeditionary Force. His military designation was No. 443288. In October 1917, Moles was ordered to re-join his company as they prepared to advance into combat. Instead of moving forward to the front lines, he fled to a rear-area village. Following a three-week evasion, he was arrested, court-martialled, found guilty of desertion, and sentenced to death. According to official British and Canadian War Diaries, the execution was carried out by a firing squad comprising Four soldiers selected from each company of the battalion, One Sergeant. Lieutenant Charles Hamilton Seaman (the officer in charge).

James Molyneaux of 1 Loyal North Lancs, was serving under a suspended sentence of 10 years’ penal servitude. His execution took place on 15 June and was the third shooting in the battalion in four months, the firing squad being found from Molyneaux’s own unit. Whilst it is difficult to imagine that there could be any consistency in a policy that generated successive executions in one particular unit, it would seem that the principle of deterrence was being exercised by HQ.

Lance-Corporal William Moon was a young volunteer in a division that had been heavily engaged before the Battle of the Somme had even commenced. Moon’s departure had been followed by a divisional move to the Armentieres front. The unfortunate twenty year old, who was serving in 11 battalion Cheshire Regiment, met his end near Bailleul.

Private Herbert Morris was a 17-year-old Jamaican soldier serving in the British Army who was executed by firing squad for desertion on 20 September 1917 after suffering from severe shell shock. He was born in Riversdale, Jamaica, and volunteered to fight in World War I, joining the 6th Battalion of the British West Indies Regiment (BWIR). While serving in the heavy artillery sectors of the Ypres Salient in Belgium, Morris became deeply traumatized and disordered by continuous bombardment (shell shock/PTSD). He ran away from his post and was later found wandering in Boulogne, France. A British military court-martial tried him for desertion from active service. The court did not adjourn the trial to seek medical reports regarding his psychological state, and Field Marshal Douglas Haig confirmed his death sentence.

Driver James Mullany (Service Number 64987) of the 72nd Battery, 38th Brigade, Royal Field Artillery, was executed by firing squad on 3 October 1916 during the First World War. He was executed for the military offence of striking a superior officer. On 16 September 1916, Mullany's Battery Sergeant Major ordered six teams of horses to be harnessed to move ammunition up to the front line. Mullany vocally protested the order, shouting, "What about some ******* tea?" When placed under open arrest, Mullany demanded close arrest so he could get his tea. When the Non-Commissioned Officer (NCO) ordered him to proceed with harnessing the horses, Mullany swore at him and was ordered to the guardroom. Mullany then physically attacked the NCO, knocking him to the ground and punching him. He was tried by a Field General Court-Martial, found guilty of striking his superior officer, and sentenced to death. He is buried at the Poperinghe New Military Cemetery in Belgium

Private Thomas Hogan (who served under the alias Thomas Murphy) was a First World War soldier executed for desertion by the British Army on 14 May 1917.  He served as a Private (Service Number 17137) in the 2nd Battalion, Royal Inniskilling Fusiliers. He was born in Tralee, County Kerry, Ireland, and was the son of John and Jane Hogan. Hogan had served in the military for over two years. He subsequently deserted his post, remaining at large until his capture. He was tried by a court-martial and sentenced to death. He was shot by a firing squad at the age of 31, making him older than the average soldier executed during the war. He was the first Irishman to be executed under British military law in 1917

Private Murphy absented himself from his unit on the Western Front and managed to evade military authorities for six months. Because he was missing for such an extensive period, a military court-martial found him guilty of intentional desertion, and his death sentence was confirmed by the high command. He was shot at dawn alongside several other Commonwealth soldiers stationed in the sector

Private Murphy had served through the majority of the war but struggled heavily with military discipline. Records indicate he was convicted of desertion on three separate occasions. His final offense occurred when he returned to his company, only to walk away the very next day while his unit was actively marching toward the front lines. According to the account of the Roman Catholic Padre who accompanied him, Murphy went to his execution by firing squad feeling "wonderfully calm"

Private William Murphy (also recorded as Murphey) was a British Army soldier who was executed for desertion on 7 February 1917 during World War I. He was a 30-year-old former coal miner from Blackridge, West Lothian, Scotland, serving with the 1/5th Battalion (attached to the 5/6th) of the Royal Scots. Murphy volunteered for service under Kitchener's recruitment campaign. He arrived in France on 28 December 1916 to join his unit on the Western Front. Just seven days after arriving, during a march toward the front lines near La Vicogne, Murphy fell out of the formation and deserted, despite the unit still being a significant distance from the actual trenches. After multiple prior military discipline infractions, he was court-martialled for desertion on active service and sentenced to death. The execution order was confirmed by Field Marshal Sir Douglas Haig. He was shot by a firing squad at dawn on 7 February 1917 at Bertrancourt, France. He is buried in the Bertrancourt Military Cemetery

Driver Robert Murray (Service Number 96498) was a British soldier who was executed by firing squad for desertion during World War I on 3 February 1917. He was one of 306 executed British and Commonwealth soldiers posthumously pardoned by the British government in 2006 under the Armed Forces Act. He served in "A" Battery, 147th Brigade, attached to the 81st Brigade of the Royal Field Artillery. Murray arrived to serve on the Western Front in France on 25 September 1915. Following a period of home leave in mid-1916, Murray went missing from his brigade. Rather than hiding near the frontlines, he managed to travel all the way to the south of France.  a domestic argument, she reported his whereabouts to the French police, who subsequently arrested him and handed him over to British military authorities.  A British military court-martial found Murray guilty of desertion and sentenced him to death. He was executed at dawn on 3 February 1917. He was shot side-by-side with Private Ernest Walter Jack Harris of the Lancashire Fusiliers, who was also executed for desertion that morning. Driver Murray is buried at the Carnoy Military Cemetery in the Somme region of France (Plot Z, Grave 10), directly next to Private Harris

Private Walter Neave was a British soldier executed for desertion during World War I on 30 August 1917. He was one of 306 soldiers executed by the British Army for disciplinary offenses who were later posthumously pardoned. He served as Private 19445 in the 10th Battalion, West Yorkshire Regiment (Prince of Wales's Own). He enlisted in April 1915 and fought in the Gallipoli campaign before being deployed to the Western Front. After being wounded on the Somme in September 1916, Neave was passed fit to return to active service. In July 1917, while already subject to a suspended death sentence for a previous instance of desertion, he decamped (deserted) again. He was executed by firing squad at dawn on 30 August 1917. Cemetery near Arras, France

Private William Nelson, 14th Durham Light Infantry, had committed his offence in the vicinity of Ypres. The court heard that he had two previous convictions for absence, for which he received a sentence of one year’s imprisonment followed by a sentence of penal servitude for life. By the time the Commander-in-Chief had determined Nelson’s fate, the private’s unit had travelled south to the Somme. He was executed at Acheux. It is interesting to note that Private Nelson’s home town of Seaham Harbour had been shelled by a German submarine on 11th July. It is not of course possible to determine whether or not the soldier was aware of this incident, nor whether his possible concern had any bearing on his actions. Shot at Dawn; Putkowski and Sykes; Leo Cooper, 1989, ISBN 0 85052 295 1. Private Billy Nelson who enlisted at the age of 17 with the 14th DLI a month after War was declared. His father had been taken prisoner in Germany at the outbreak of war aboard the collier Seaham Harbour and shortly after signing up he lost his mother, leaving him responsible for his sister Norah aged 13, and brother Harry aged 10. Having endured some of the bloodiest horrors of the conflict whilst fighting at Ypres, young Billy went absent without leave on the anniversary of his mother’s death and again went missing two months later. Deeply disturbed and clearly in need of help he was instead court martialled, field punished and sentenced to death. 5.15am 11th August 1916

Private Charles Bain Nicholson was a British soldier executed by firing squad for desertion during World War I. He was shot at dawn on 27 October 1917 at the age of 19. Originally from Middlesbrough, Nicholson lied about his age to enlist at 16, joining the 8th Battalion, York and Lancaster Regiment. During a heavy bombing raid, he panicked and went missing from his platoon. His court martial lasted less than ten minutes. His platoon sergeant gave evidence against him, while Nicholson’s only defence was an 11-word statement: "When the bomb dropped, I got nervous. I can't say anything else." His military superiors ordered his execution to serve as an example to other soldiers. He is buried at the Longuenesse (St. Omer) Souvenir Cemetery in France

Private Joseph Nisbet had accrued two convictions, one for violence for which he had received a four year sentence, and another for disobedience for which he had been sentenced to death. During the summer of 1918 Nisbet had reported sick at a time when the battalion had been warned for the front line. He was ordered to attend the next sick parade, but instead he absconded. Three days later he was arrested in Calais without his equipment. In confirming the sentence of death, no doubt the Commander-in-Chief took into consideration the opinion of the man’s CO, who had reported that the private’s behaviour might well prove infectious.

Private Benjamin O'Connell was a young Irish soldier serving in the British Army during World War I who was executed by firing squad for desertion. He was one of 306 British and Commonwealth soldiers "shot at dawn" for military offences who later received posthumous pardons. Private Benjamin O'Connell (Service Number 10686), 1st Battalion, Irish Guards. Born in Waterford, he lived in Tinnarath, Foulksmills, County Wexford, Ireland. He was the son of James and Mary O'Connell. August 8, 1918. Age at Death: 23 or 24 years old. He was executed for desertion. Reports indicate he left his post to "find a woman", making him the fifth and final member of the Irish Guards to be executed during the war. O'Connell was one of 26 Irish-born British soldiers executed during the Great War for breaches of military discipline.

Unit: 1st Battalion Notts and Derby Regiment (Sherwood Foresters)
Notes: Private Frank O’Neill, Sherwood Foresters was executed at dawn for desertion. He had two previous convictions. He was the last man to be unrepresented at his trial. He was offered a half pint of brandy before being shot but declined.

Private Anthony Victor O'Neill (sometimes spelled Neil) was a British soldier executed by firing squad for desertion during World War I on 30 April 1916.  Private Anthony Victor O'Neill, service number 1/15134, served with the 1st Battalion, South Wales Borderers. He was a "Kitchener volunteer" from Neath, Wales. He was 20 years old at the time of his death. He was court-martialled and condemned under the Army Act for desertion. He is buried at the Mazingarbe Communal Cemetery Extension in the Nord-Pas-de-Calais region of France

Henry Palmer was charged with constructive desertion for at least three instances of being absent from his unit. He entered a not guilty plea, to each of the three charges. The first two charges he was found not guilty, mainly because of insufficient evidence. His unit had been heavily involved in the Battle of Morval on the 25th September and on the 1st October 1916, just south of Le Sars. Henry was found not guilty of the two earlier offences, which occurred in late September, but the third charge, on the 1st and 2nd October, he was found guilty and condemned to death. At Henry’s trial prosecution witnesses were not cross-examined. Palmer told the court that he advanced in the attack but that he had been hit in the knee. However, he was unable to remember his whereabouts at the time of his alleged injury. He stated at first he was hit halfway across No Man’s Land, later he said he was hit in front of the German Wire. In his first version of events, Palmer stated that after being hit he returned and stopped in a communication trench to have a rest. He could not find his unit on the following day, due to the heavy shelling. When further questioned, he agreed that his injury had not caused him to report sick. Also he remarked that he threw his ammunition away when injured near the German Wire. He then returned to the British front line. Henry Palmer was unrepresented and said very little in his defence. He also called no witnesses and did not ask any questions. This was noted by the court at the time. The findings of the Court were passed up the Chain of Command. Lt General W P Pulteney, Corps Commander had noted: The Battalion fought well (in the action from which Palmer was absent) and has good discipline. I support the recommendation of the court: ‘mercy’. There is an additional note that reads There appears to be no need for an example to be made. Sir Henry Rawlinson General, commanding the Fourth Army, confirmed his support for the Death Penalty, which was also confirmed by Field Marshal Haig using in his green fountain pen)Confirmed.

Rifleman Albert Parker serving with 7 King’s Royal Rifle Corps. His crime was a typical example of desertion committed with the intention of avoiding service in the line. 35 year old Parker admitted drunkenness at his trial but this did not mitigate his offence. An eyewitness later recalled the promulgation of sentence and the execution that followed. ‘Then the prisoner’s cap was taken off, [this ritual is laid down in King’s Regulations No.481, the cap being removed to prevent its possible use as a missile] and he was told to take one pace forward, which he did. Then the APM commenced to read the papers … ‘The man was then told to take a pace back again, which he did without a quiver – a braver man at that moment wasn't to be found in France. He was then marched away to the place where he was to be shot. We were then ordered to about turn, and the Brigade Transport Officer threatened us that any man who turned round would be put on a crime. So we stood in silence for what seemed hours, although only minutes. Then the shots rang out and one of the Yorkshires fainted, the strain was that great. [A man from the 6th Battalion King’s Own Yorkshire Light Infantry.] Still we stood in silence until we heard another shot, which I afterwards ascertained was the doctor’s shot to make sure he was dead.’ [The writer means the coup de grâce administered by the officer commanding the firing squad.] The execution took place at Warlus, where Albert Parker, a Watford man, was buried in the Communal Cemetery – the only soldier’s grave – dating from the Great War. His headstone now carries the inscription, ‘Gone but not forgotten’.

Private Albert Parry from 2 West Yorks. Little is known about Parry except than he was a deserter, and the eighth soldier to be executed in his division (8 Division). His army number would suggest that he was a conscript. It must be presumed from his place of burial that the execution took place in a remote spot behind Armentières – within yards of the Franco-Belgian border.

Private Pattison served on the Western Front with 7 East Surreys, and it was recorded that he was the first soldier in his unit to suffer from shellshock. The onset of Pattison’s disability is recorded to have occurred on 5 March 1916, and it is not difficult to visualise his predicament, given that at the time his unit was serving opposite the Hohenzollern Redoubt. This area was the scene of constant mining and counter mining as the belligerents cratered the wasteland in vain and bloody attempts to gain a slight territorial advantage. The battalion diarist gave a graphic account of hostilities in the week following the private’s illness. The diarist recorded that on 6 March the Germans put down a heavy bombardment, and just after midnight they exploded a mine under the trenches to the right of the British line. The following night the enemy made three raids against the British front line. On 10 March, the enemy carried out a night-time bombing raid, which was followed the next night by the detonation of another mine. At the end of the week the British ‘blew in’ three German mineshafts during defensive operations. If such conditions were typical, then it is not surprising that men succumbed to shellshock. It is not known on what date Private Pattison returned to duty, but what is surprising, given the soldier’s shellshocked condition, is that during the very same month (March), he was convicted of desertion and sentenced to 84 days’ field punishment no. 1. Somehow Pattison managed to maintain control of his nerves for over a year – until the Battle of Arras loomed. On 2 April 1917 his battalion went into the front line, and a week later were in action on the first day of battle. The soldier stuck it, but on 3 May prior to an attack, his nerves gave way. He reported to the battalion doctor, whose examination culminated with instructions to return to the line. It would be an understatement to say that the medic failed in his duty. One time army doctor Lord Moran described how during the war he came to judge when a man was finished, when a soldier could no longer be of any use until rested and recovered. On 4 May Private Pattison was arrested by the military police in Arras. The account given by the policeman at the court martial indicated that Pattison was displaying symptoms of shellshock. It is not known whether Private Pattison was medically examined whilst in confinement, but if he was, then the medical profession once again failed to recognise the soldier’s confused condition. Privates Pattison was shot at Arras on 4 July.

Private Major Penn (1st Battalion, Royal Welch Fusiliers) was a British soldier executed for desertion on April 22, 1915, during the First World War. He and a comrade, Private Albert Troughton, were found guilty of leaving their posts and were executed together by a firing squad on April 22, 1915. Penn and Troughton endured heavy bombardments and saw hundreds of their comrades killed. Under intense pressure, the men became separated from their unit. Following a court-martial, the men were sentenced to death. The night before his execution, Private Troughton reportedly smuggled a letter out to his family, stating he would "die like a soldier"

Private Eugène Perry (born Eugène Poirier) was a Canadian World War I soldier who was executed by firing squad for desertion on 11 April 1917. Born on 1 April 1896 in Bouctouche, New Brunswick, he enlisted in the military using the alias Eugene Perry. He served with the 22nd Battalion (French Canadian), commonly known as the "Van Doos". On 2 April 1917, Perry was ordered to report for duty in the front-line trenches. He went missing and was arrested seven hours later in a village located approximately 20 miles behind the front lines. A military court-martial found him guilty of desertion and sentenced him to death. He was executed on 11 April 1917, just two days after the historic Canadian assault on Vimy Ridge. He was the first of five soldiers from the 22nd Battalion to be executed during the war. His remains are interred at the Écoivres Military Cemetery in France

Private Louis Phillips lived in the West End of London – although he had been born at Caistor, and chose to serve in the Somerset Light Infantry. In April 1915 he went to France with a draft of men destined for 6 Battalion who were serving in the Ypres Salient. During sustained and bloody fighting at the end of July he went absent for four days. At his court martial he said in mitigation that he had not received any letters from home for several weeks prior to committing his offence, and that this had caused him grievous concern. Sentencing him to death the court added a recommendation for mercy, on the grounds that Phillips had been suffering from mental worry. Scant consideration was given to this recommendation and, at 4.20 am on 19 August, the Ramparts at Ypres were the scene of yet another execution. Strangely this 23 year old volunteer is not recorded in the official casualty records – Soldiers Died in the Great War. Yet the only other soldier from the regiment to be executed (in 1916) is commemorated. A cover-up seems likely because Louis Phillips’ death certificate records that he was killed in action. The soldier is also commemorated in the British Jewry Book of Honour.

Private William Henry Thomas Henry Phillips was a British soldier executed for desertion during World War I. Service Number: 9197, Regiment: 1st Battalion, Bedfordshire Regiment. Date of Execution: 30 May 1916. Cause of Death: Shot at dawn by firing squad after a military court-martial. Burial Location: He is buried in the northwest part of the Wormhoudt Communal Cemetery in Nord, France

Private Albert Henry Pitts was a British soldier who was executed by firing squad for desertion during World War I. He was shot at dawn on 8 February 1915 at 7:30 am in Belgium. The background of his case reveals a tragic sequence of events during the early months of the conflict. Private Pitts (Service Number 8747) served with the 2nd Battalion, Royal Warwickshire Regiment. He was an experienced "old soldier," having previously completed 12 years of service with the regiment before working as a drayman and re-enlisting at the outbreak of the war in 1914. In late 1914, Pitts became separated from his unit. In letters sent to his wife in Bengeworth, Evesham, he explained that he had been lost for two weeks and was struggling to find his regiment because he could not understand the French directions. He also mentioned that he had gone completely deaf, a common side-effect of artillery shell shock. Despite his letters indicating an intention to rejoin his unit, his absence during Christmas was treated as intentional. He was court-martialled for desertion and executed shortly thereafter. Because he was executed, he does not have a traditional Commonwealth War Grave; instead, his name is commemorated on the Ploegsteert Memorial in Belgium

Second Lieutenant Eric Skeffington Poole was the first British commissioned officer executed by military authority during World War I. A shell-shock sufferer, he was found guilty of desertion by a Field General Court Martial and shot by a firing squad at Poperinghe, Belgium, on December 10, 1916. During the Battle of the Somme, Poole was knocked unconscious and buried by an enemy shell, subsequently suffering from shell shock (now known as PTSD). Following recuperation, he returned to the front lines. In a confused and disoriented state, he wandered away from his unit near Flers. He was arrested days later and charged with desertion. Despite pleas for leniency from several commanding officers due to his mental state, the death sentence was confirmed by Field Marshal Douglas Haig. Poole was executed at 7:25 AM behind the Poperinghe town hall. He is buried in the Poperinghe New Military Cemetery in Belgium

Private Harry Poole was a British soldier executed by firing squad for desertion during World War I on 9 December 1916. Private Harry Poole (Service Number 8534), serving in the 7th Battalion, Yorkshire Regiment. He was a 22-year-old former working-class miner from Sheffield. He escaped from military detention on 24 October 1916 and spent roughly six weeks on the run. He was re-arrested in Boulogne around 22 November 1916, court-martialled, and sentenced to death. He was "shot at dawn" on 9 December 1916.  He is buried at the Cavillon Communal Cemetery in France.

Corporal George Henry Povey was a British soldier executed by firing squad for "quitting his post" during World War I. He is historically significant as the first Welshman to be executed by the British Army during the conflict. On 28 January 1915, while serving with the 1st Battalion, Cheshire Regiment, Corporal Povey was in charge of a frontline trench section in the Ypres Salient. A German soldier allegedly crept close and pulled a rifle out of a loophole, triggering a false alarm. In the ensuing panic, someone shouted "Clear out, lads, they're on us," prompting Povey and several privates to retreat toward the support trenches. Povey was stopped at a support point, still in possession of all his arms and equipment, and immediately returned to the frontline when ordered. He was court-martialled alongside the privates. While the other men received lesser or commuted sentences, Field Marshal Sir John French confirmed the death penalty for Povey, reportedly to make an example of him because of his rank as a non-commissioned officer. He was shot at dawn at 7:45 am on 11 February 1915 at the age of 23. The execution took place in St Jans Cappel, France. He was led from a cell in nearby Poperinge, Belgium, to face the firing squad. He has no known grave; records of where his body was buried did not survive the war

Unit: 10th Battalion Notts and Derby's Regiment (Sherwood Foresters)
Notes: Gallipoli veteran, Pte. William Henry Randle, 10th Battalion Nottinghamshire & Derbyshire Regiment (formerly 9th Battalion), was executed for desertion on 25th November 1916. Born in Hucknall, he lived on Wollaton Street until moving to Shirebrook with his family before the outbreak of war. When he was arrested, Randle claimed that he was looking for his brother, who was said to be serving nearby. His defence was not accepted and he was sentenced to death, a sentence that was not commuted – unlike 90% of such punishments. Buried in Cavillon Communal Cemetery, he was the 23 year-old son of William Henry and Harriett Randle, of 26 Vale Drive, Shirebrook.

Corporal James Reid (Service Number 7674) of the 6th Battalion, Cameron Highlanders was a British soldier executed for desertion during World War I. He was shot by a firing squad at dawn on 11 May 1918 at the age of 26. Reid was already a serving soldier when the war broke out in 1914 and had a record of serving well through the early years of the conflict. He was slightly wounded twice during his first two years of active duty. His record shifted in August 1916 when he deserted for the first time, resulting in a suspended prison sentence. Though later promoted to corporal, he deserted again in the spring of 1917, living behind the lines until French police arrested him that September. While locked in a regimental guard room awaiting his court-martial in October 1917, Reid broke out and managed to evade military authorities for four months. Reid was eventually recaptured and court-martialled. Although the court recommended mercy based on his prior years of good frontline service, the high-ranking confirming authorities rejected the plea to make an example of him. He was executed in the spring of 1918. He is buried at the Duisans British Cemetery in Etrun, France

Private Isaac Reid (Service Number 8752) of the 2nd Battalion, Scots Guards, was a British soldier executed for desertion during World War I. He was shot by a firing squad at dawn on 9 April 1915 in Laventie, France. Reid deserted his post during the fierce Battle of Neuve Chapelle in March 1915. Military police discovered him hiding in the rear lines a few hours after his disappearance. During his trial, Reid was unrepresented by legal counsel. He admitted that he "lost his head" in the chaos of battle and expressed deep regret. Although his superiors noted he had a "very good" character, they also reported he was "not a good fighter". Despite a formal recommendation for mercy, the death sentence was upheld as a military deterrent. On the morning of 9 April 1915, Reid was tied to a tree across the green at Laventie and shot. His own company commander led the firing squad, which was comprised of regimental snipers. The remaining Guards were forced to parade and watch the execution. Reid's execution deeply humiliated F Company. Shamed by his desertion, the men vowed never to surrender in battle to restore their company's honour. Just over a month later, at the Battle of Festubert on 16 May 1915, 80 men from F Company were entirely cut off by German forces. True to their word, they refused to yield and died to a man.Author Stephen Graham documented the incident in his 1919 memoir, A Private in the Guards. He noted that the strict Company Sergeant Major who originally reported Reid for desertion became a pariah. When that Sergeant Major was later mortally wounded at Festubert, his own men strictly refused to give him a drink of water as he lay dying. Reid is buried at the Longuenesse (St. Omer) Souvenir Cemetery in the Pas de Calais region of France

Rifleman Edward James Reynolds was born on 2 January 1896 in Toronto. In April 1915, Reynolds enlisted in the 35th Battalion. By November 1915, Reynolds was a member of the 3rd Battalion in the line near Ploegsteert.On 25 July 1916, the Germans exploded a mine under a portion of the front line called “The Bluff”. The 3rd Battalion was ordered forward to plug the resulting gap in the front line. However, Reynolds fell out from his platoon only to be found 2 days later at his battalion’s transport lines. Reynolds claimed that he had been ordered back and got lost. This excuse was accepted. During the following night (26 July 1916), Reynolds was ordered to accompany a ration party up to the front line. Again Reynolds fell out and went back to his battalion’s transport lines. This time Reynolds was arrested and charged with desertion. He was found guilty by a court-martial and sentenced to death. At 05:27 on 23 August 1916, Reynolds (aged 20) was executed by firing squad. His remains are now located in Longuenesse Souvenir Cemetery, Plot IV, Row A, Grave 39. It is of interest that both the Toronto Star and the Toronto Telegram reported at the time that Reynolds had been killed in action. In 2001, the Canadian government added the names of those executed for desertion and cowardice during the war to the Book of Remembrance at Parliament Hill.

Malcolm Richmond had escaped from the guardroom at Etaples on 14 October 1917, only a short while after the Etaples disturbances had died down. A month later he had been arrested in nearby Boulogne, when he had given false particulars. Richmond proved a slippery customer and he escaped again in December, gaining yet another month’s liberty. Early in 1918 he was again arrested in Boulogne after trying to bluff his way free. The matter did not end there however, as a fortnight later he escaped again, only to be arrested a day later masquerading as a driver in the Army Service Corps. Yet another false story would suggest that Private Richmond was an inveterate liar, and Anthony Babington comments that enquiries made by the military failed to determine that the soldier had ever been an inmate of an asylum.43 22 year old Richmond, who was serving in 1/6 Gordon Highlanders, part of 51 Division, was shot near Arras. His death was the final execution in the Highland Division. Another 22 year old from the north of England was shot the next day.

Private Albert Rickman was a British soldier who was executed by firing squad for desertion during World War I. He was shot at 6:10 am on 15 September 1916 in Vlamertinge, Belgium, at the age of 27. He served with the 1st Battalion, Royal Dublin Fusiliers (Service Number: 12923). He volunteered early in August 1914 following Lord Kitchener's call to arms. He originally served in the 7th Battalion and fought in the Gallipoli campaign, where he was wounded and evacuated back to England before recovering and being sent to France. Suffering from severe battle fatigue and grief over losing his close friends, Rickman and a companion slipped away from their unit during the brutal Somme campaign. They attempted to flee to the coast to sneak aboard a ship back to England, with the misguided plan of joining the Royal Navy. He was arrested on 20 July 1916 behind the lines. At his court martial, he pleaded for leniency, citing his previous good conduct and the trauma of losing his friends, but his actions were deemed a deliberate act of desertion. The death sentence was passed down and ultimately confirmed by the Commander-in-Chief of the British Expeditionary Force, Sir Douglas Haig, on 12 September 1916. Because his death was classified as ignominious, he was denied military honours at his funeral, his medals were forfeited, and his grieving mother was denied a war gratuity pension. Rickman was buried at the Vlamertinghe Military Cemetery in West-Vlaanderen, Belgium

The circumstances leading up to the General Court Martial of Private Thomas Henry Basil Rigby, In the Field is as follows:- At about 3 pm on the afternoon of Tuesday 31 July 1917, when 10th (Service) Battalion, South Wales Borderers was at Kiel Cot (Old German Front Line), instructions were received that No1 Platoon was to supply four men to act as Brigade Runners.  Four soldiers from the Platoon were detailed for this task, including Private Rigby.  He was last seen by the other members of this unit at 11 am on Thursday 2 August 1917. At 11.20 am on Tuesday 7 August 1917, Lance Corporal Kirby of the Military Field Police was on duty in Boulevard Jacquard, Calais, when he had cause to stop and question Private Rigby.  On being asked which unit he belonged to Rigby said, The King’s Liverpool Regiment.  He was not in possession of a Pass authorising him to be in the town, he also had no shoulder or cap badges on show.  He was therefore arrested and taken to Rue Leonard de Vinci Police Billet, Calais. When later interviewed Rigby gave his name as Private 28075 Thomas Lee, 19th Battalion, King’s Liverpool Regiment.  He stated that he was from St. Martin’s Camp in Boulogne and had left there on Saturday 4 August 1917.  He was not in possession of a Pay Book, Identity Discs or Regimental Badges.  Not being satisfied with his explanation Rigby was detained at Fort Risban Guard House, Calais. When further interviewed he admitted that he had supplied false personal details, stating that he was in fact Private Harry Rigby of 10th (Service) Battalion, South Wales Borderers. The Court Martial of Private Kirby took place on Monday 22 October 1917.  The President of the Court was a Major T H Morgan, with members Captain E A Singleton and Captain I A Morgan. Offence Charged:  ‘When on active service deserting His Majesty’s Service, in that you Private No. 11490 Rigby, a Soldier of the Regular Forces , in the field on 2 August 1917, absented yourself from the 10th (Service) Battalion, South Wales Borderers, until apprehended by the Military Police on 7 August 1917’. He pleaded ‘Not Guilty’.  Following the Prosecution case, Private Rigby elected not to give oral evidence but in stead supplied a written statement which read –  Gentlemen.  I was detailed by Sergeant Green at about 2.30 pm on 31 July 1917 as a Runner for Brigade.  This was at Kiel Cot.  I went to Brigade along with Private Johnson and six other men.  The Corporal in charge was Corporal Watling, but he was wounded in the wrist before he arrived at Brigade Headquarters.  I do not remember anything which happened to me after about 12 noon on 2 August until I came to my senses on the outskirts of a town called Watou on the 6 August.  I made my way towards the railway where I saw a freight car, with not knowing which way the line ran.  I thought the train was coming towards Poperinghe.  Whilst in the train I fell asleep, and when I awoke the train was in a siding at Calais.  I did not know that it was Calais at the time until I got into the town.  I am sorry this has happened but I must have been partially mad at the time through worrying about my wife.  I was married on the 21 September 1915 and sent out to the front on the 29th of the same month, and I have not seen my wife since.  Gentlemen, I remain your honourable servant. Harry Rigby.  The Court was informed that Private Rigby was under a suspended sentence of 3 years penal servitude for previous desertion. He was found guilty of desertion.  The sentence of the court was that he suffer death by being shot. The sentence was carried out at 6.40 am on 22 November 1917.

John Roberts of 2 Canadian Mounted Rifles. J W Muirhead, a young officer recently commissioned into the Army Service Corps, recorded the case and its unusual twist of fate. ‘… in June 19161 went to France and landed at Havre. I was soon sent to Boulogne where I spent a month. While I was there I was detailed to be an officer in waiting at a court martial which was hearing a case of desertion. The prisoner was a Canadian of 19 years, and as a volunteer had been sent to France with his regiment from which he had deserted and found his way to Boulogne. Here he got entangled with a woman with whom he lived for several months. He might never have been arrested if he had not drawn his pay regularly from the Base Cashier. He was sentenced to death and three weeks later he was shot …’  Robert’s long absence undoubtedly influenced the decision to confirm his sentence; as during this time he had avoided the carnage suffered by his battalion in the operations to recover Observatory Ridge in the Ypres Salient. His mother received a blunt notification of her son’s demise. ‘Madam, With deep regret I have the honour to inform you that a report has been received to the effect that no. 107526, Private Roberts J W was tried by Field General Court-Martial at Boulogne, France on the 15th day of July, 1916, on the charge of “when on active service deserting His Majesty’s Service” and was sentenced by the Court “to suffer death by being shot.” The sentence was duly carried out at 4.36 a. m. on the 30th day of July, 1916. I have the honour to be, Madam, Your obedient servant, Frank Beard i/c Record Office.’ The first soldier to be executed in August 1916 was yet another Canadian, of obvious French descent.

William Roberts, known as Ted to his relatives, was drafted to 4 Royal Fusiliers in November 1914. His service was exemplary and on 16 June 1915 he was severely wounded in the head during an attack at Hooge in the Ypres Salient. Private Roberts was one of 369 casualties suffered by his battalion that day. After treatment and convalescence, the soldier returned on 20 September 1915 to his battalion, which was still in the Ypres Salient, in an area known as Sanctuary Wood. Five days later, bloody fighting broke out in the Salient as the British High Command attempted to draw enemy attention away from the Loos offensive – then taking place to the south. As the diversionary attacks slackened Private Roberts slipped away from his battalion in the front line trenches at Hooge Crater. Unlike those who fled in the direction of the Channel Ports, Roberts remained just a short distance behind the lines. For quite a while he avoided drawing attention to himself until he was arrested on 4 May 1916 in the village of Brandhoek – just west of Ypres. While under arrest Private Roberts was kept in secure confinement at Locre, a small village on the Franco-Belgian border, but on 9 May he escaped – only to be re-arrested shortly afterwards. On 20 May he stood trial at Locre before a court martial staffed by a lieutenant- colonel and three captains. Roberts’ Commanding Officer described the Londoner as a good and plucky soldier, telling the court that the private had volunteered for dangerous tasks on a number of occasions. It is difficult to imagine what better testimonial could have been given. Nevertheless the reviewing authorities wasted little time, Sir Douglas Haig confirming the sentence a week later. It must be presumed that Roberts’ length of absence, coupled with his escape, had negated the private’s previous good service, and from a military view point he was now valueless. At 3.45 am on 29 May a firing squad created another unfortunate ‘example’, the Medical Officer blandly recording that Roberts ‘died of gunshot wounds’. In the early 1980s a story emerged that Private Roberts had been shot for habitually stealing the rum ration and drinking it himself. It would seem that the story was concocted to cover family embarrassment about this regrettable incident.

Sergeant John Robins (Service No. 9610) was a soldier in the 5th Battalion, Wiltshire Regiment during World War I. He was executed by a British firing squad at Gallipoli on January 2, 1916, for disobeying a lawful command.  In December 1915 at Suvla, Robins was ordered by a junior officer to join a reconnaissance patrol. He refused the order, citing severe ill health. Robins maintained that he was too sick to carry out the duty, but his medical reports failed to validate the severity of his condition. Found guilty of wilful defiance of a lawful command, Robins was demoted to Private and sentenced to death. He faced the firing squad at 8:05 AM on Gully Beach. He is buried in the Twelve Tree Copse Cemetery in Turkey

Private Arthur Harold Robinson was a British soldier executed by firing squad for desertion on 10 May 1916during World War I. He served as Private 15469 in the 9th Battalion, Northumberland Fusiliers. He was from Eckington, near Sheffield, and was the son of Mrs. Sarah Ann Robinson. Robinson had served for approximately 10 months on the Western Front. Records indicate he deserted while already serving a suspended 10-year sentence of penal servitude for a previous desertion offence. He was court-martialled, sentenced to death, and executed at the age of 24. He is buried at the Cité Bonjean Military Cemetery in Armentières, France

Private John Robinson (7377) 3rd Battalion Worcestershire Regiment. Private Robinson of Nechells, Birmingham was a regular soldier with 13 years previous service and had been with the 3rd Battalion since Mons in August 1914. On the 27th June 1915, Private Robinson and Private Alfred Thompson absconded together after they were told that they were to be on night duty in trenches near Hooge. The 3rd Battalion had been in action in this area since 16th June. On the 5th July 1915 both Private Robinson and Private Thompson were arrested at Abancourt while they were sitting on a train bound for Rouen. At their court martial in a statement it said that both men were good soldiers, but that it appeared they were suffering from nervous strain at the time they went absent. Robinson was shot by firing squad with 4 other deserters from the 3rd Battalion on the ramparts of Ypres on the 26th July 1915. He was 31 years of age. He was originally buried at the Ramparts Cemetery but was later transferred to the Aeroplane Cemetery, Belgium, which is 3.5 Km northeast of Ypres town centre (Grave number II.A.6/7). the grave of Robinson has the following inscription: "In loving memory of my dear son deeply mourned by father mother, sisters and brothers".

Unit: 1st Battalion Notts and Derby's Regiment (Sherwood Foresters)
Notes: Private William Robinson (Service Number: 70715), who served with the 1st Battalion of the Sherwood Foresters (Nottinghamshire and Derbyshire Regiment), was executed by firing squad for desertion during World War I on April 10, 1917. He is buried at the Péronne Communal Cemetery Extension in France. He was charged with desertion. He had gone missing in early March 1917, shortly before a planned attack, to avoid taking part in it. He was tried in March 1917 and executed at dawn on April 10, 1917, the day after the opening of the Battle of Arras

Unit: 2nd Battalion King's Own Yorkshire Light Infantry
Notes: George Ernest Roe was born in 1894, Sheffield, Yorkshire. He was the son of John L Roe and Mary Wells.In 1911 Geoge’s occupation was a Labourer aged 17. He lived with his family at 16 Alfred Road, Brightside, Sheffield, Yorkshire. George joined the King’s Own Yorkshire Light Infantry (KOYLI) 2nd Battalion. Rank Private. Regimental No. 3/1433. Private George Ernest Roe was executed by a firing squad for desertion on 11th June 1915 aged 19. He is buried at Perth Cemetery China Wall, Belgium.  His battalion had seen heavy fighting & suffered huge casualties in the Ypres Salient. He was undefended at trial, where he was given a good character, but said to have lost his nerve. On 7 November 2006, the UK government announced retrospective pardons for all British personnel executed during the Great War. There seems to be a discrepancy about his age as he was almost 21 when he was executed. But the information from the CWGC have him down as 19. Some young soldiers did lie about their age in order for them to join the army. However, it is worth noting that he was in the regular army at the time of his death

Private John Rogers was a British soldier who was executed by firing squad for desertion during World War I on 9 March 1917. He was one of the 306 British and Commonwealth military personnel "Shot at Dawn" during the conflict, and he was later granted a posthumous pardon by the British Ministry of Defence. Private Rogers (Service Number 26028) served with the 2nd Battalion, South Lancashire Regiment. Unusually for desertion cases, he absconded while his unit was actively serving in the front-line trenches. At his military trial, Rogers argued that he suffered from mental confusion. He claimed he had been so highly intoxicated the night before his disappearance that he was incapable of rational action or intent. The court-martial rejected his defence, convicted him, and sentenced him to death.

Private Frederick Rose (Service No. 9552) was a regular British Army soldier who was executed for desertion during World War I on 4 March 1917. He was one of the 306 British and Commonwealth soldiers "Shot at Dawn" for military offences who later received posthumous pardons. Born in 1892 or 1894 in Chelsea, London. 2nd Battalion, Alexandra, Princess of Wales's Own (Yorkshire Regiment)—commonly known as the Green Howards. He enlisted as a regular soldier in 1909 and served as a Drummer and Private. He deployed to Europe with his battalion at the very start of the war in 1914. Private Rose went missing from his unit on 18 December 1914 during active operations in Belgium. Instead of returning to his regiment, he successfully evaded authorities for approximately two years by living with a French woman in the town of Hazebrouck, France. He was eventually discovered and arrested after a neighbour reported him to the local French police. During his Field General Court Martial, Rose referenced family issues to explain his absence, but his lengthy two-year evasion meant he was given the death penalty for desertion. He was shot by a firing squad at dawn on 4 March 1917, aged 23 or 25

Private Samuel Sabongidda who was serving in 3 Nigerian Regiment. The exact nature of his crime is unknown, however Sabongidda was shot for an offence involving violence. The condemned man had served in the army since September 1914, and was the only soldier from his regiment to be executed during the war. In the second half of 1917 two other soldiers were also shot for offences of violence. Both men were from the same regiment whose battalions were serving in the Middle East. The unit concerned was the British West Indies Regiment, and the first offender was a particularly rebellious and vicious individual.

Private Harry Salter was a British soldier executed for desertion during World War I. He was shot at dawn on 11 December 1915 at the age of 24. Born in Bridgwater, Somerset, Salter was orphaned by age 14. He experienced poverty and served a sentence in a Borstal institution for petty crime before the war. He joined the 6th Battalion, East Lancashire Regiment and deployed to Gallipoli in July 1915, enduring brutal front-line conditions and widespread disease. In August 1915, he was given a 12-month suspended prison sentence for a previous instance of absence. On 1 November 1915, Salter walked away from his battalion. Over the next two weeks, he was arrested multiple times but escaped from his military escorts repeatedly. When final custody was secured on 19 November, he was caught wearing an Australian uniform. At his trial, Salter offered no self-defence. His commanding officer provided a negative character testimony, labeling him a bad influence. General Charles Monro confirmed the death sentence. He is buried at the Green Hill Cemetery in Gallipoli, Turkey.

Irish lance corporal Peter Sands was shot as a deserter at Fleurbaix, near Armentières. Sands, a nine-year veteran age 26 or 27, left the Royal Irish Rifles with another soldier on a home leave pass in February 1915 and returned to his family in Belfast. Sands had a pass for four days. Instead, he stayed for five months — openly living with his wife, and wearing his military uniform, until some unknown busybody turned him in as a deserter that July. He would tell his court-martial that he had lost his travel documents to return to the horrible front, and had been blown off when he visited a Belfast barracks to see about a replacement. He did not aim to desert, he insisted; “Had I intended to desert I would have worn plain clothes, but up to that time I was arrested I always wore uniform.” His commanding officer “consider[ed] this a bad case of desertion and I recommend that the sentence be carried out.” And it was. Sands was buried at a nearby churchyard, but his resting-place was lost during the war. He has a marker at Cabaret-Rouge Military Cemetery at Souchez.

Private William Scholes (Service Number 44174) of the 2nd Battalion, South Wales Borderers was executed for desertion during the First World War on 8 August 1918. He was the last man serving in a Welsh regiment to be shot at dawn during the conflict. Scholes was a conscripted soldier born in 1893. At the time of his execution, he was already serving a suspended death sentence for a previous instance of desertion. Historical accounts indicate that Scholes repeatedly went absent without leave because he felt the military allowance provided to his widowed mother—for whom he was the sole financial support—was measly and inadequate. He is buried at the Borre British Cemetery in Nord, France

Private William Scotton was a British soldier executed by firing squad for desertion during the First World War. He was shot at 7:05 a.m. on 3 February 1915 in Vierstraat, Belgium, at the age of 22. He served as a Private (Service Number S/6922) in the 4th Battalion, Middlesex Regiment. Scotton initially joined the King's Liverpool Regiment in 1910 but was discharged in 1911 as "not likely to become an efficient soldier" after a prior desertion incident. He re-enlisted alongside his brother, Albert, at the outbreak of war in July 1914 and was deployed to France by December 1914. On 27 December 1914, he absented himself while his unit was relieving another regiment in the trenches before Kemmel. He was quickly caught and given 21 days of Field Punishment No. 1. On 23 January 1915, Scotton went missing again after being warned for a fatigue party moving from the reserve trenches to the frontline. He turned himself in on 25 January 1915 once his battalion returned to camp.  He was tried by a Field General Court Martial on 28 January 1915 and charged with "Deserting His Majesty's service" while on active service. Following the confirmation of his death sentence, he was executed at Vierstraat. To serve as a warning to others ("pour encourager les autres"), his own battalion was paraded to witness the firing squad, which was composed of a sergeant and seven members of his own company. Because he was executed, he has no known individual standard military grave; instead, his name is commemorated on Panel 51 of the Ypres (Menin Gate) Memorial in Belgium.

Private John Seymour (Service Number 10603) was a British soldier executed for desertion during the First World War on 24 January 1918. Private Seymour was court-martialled for desertion. At his trial, he could provide no excuse for his absence other than stating, "my nerves get the better of me sometimes". The four-man court-martial was unmoved by his plea and sentenced him to death. According to a 2004 Irish Government report, Seymour's Regimental Sergeant Major held a highly negative view of his "fighting character". This heavily influenced the confirmation process. Evidence indicates he was explicitly executed to serve as a harsh example to others because previous desertions in the unit had not been dealt with as severely. His execution was the only one carried out by the British military during the entire month of January 1918.  He is buried at the Ferme-Olivier Cemetery in Belgium

Private Frederick Sheffield was an English soldier executed by a British military firing squad for desertion during World War I. He was tried alongside another soldier and became one of the earliest men to be "shot at dawn" during the conflict. He served as a Private (Service No. 6351 / L/14164) in the 2nd Battalion, Middlesex Regiment. After six weeks of active service, Sheffield and a fellow soldier named Joseph Ball deserted their unit together in late 1914.  He was tried by a Field General Court Martial on 30 December 1914 and convicted of attempting to desert. He was executed by firing squad on 12 January 1915 in France. Because he was executed for a disciplinary offence, his name is commemorated on Panels 31 and 32 of the Le Touret Memorial in Pas de Calais, France

Private William Simmonds who had been serving in 23 Middlesex Regiment. Details of the offence conformed to a familiar pattern. Following the soldier’s absence whilst on the Somme, the private had been arrested, tried and then executed at Poperinghe. The 23 year old was the first soldier to be executed during the war whilst serving with 41 Division. On 4 December another Territorial soldier was executed; and his army number suggests that he enlisted prior to the outbreak of war. Perhaps surprisingly, only five weeks had passed since a previous death sentence had been carried out on a volunteer serving in this battalion. And by coincidence, exactly one month had passed since the last Terrier’ had been shot.

Private Robert Simmers had joined the Royal Scots and was attached to the second battalion, part of 3 Division. The 25 year old was shot on 19 May, becoming the twenty-third victim of the firing squad in this the bloodiest of all the army’s divisions, as far as death sentences were concerned. Two days later a Canadian soldier of a similar age was shot, and it is suggested that the former labourer might not have been too bright. When the man enlisted, either he did not know how old he was, or he did not know his correct date of birth. Army records of the soldier’s stated age and his date of birth do not tally.

Private Dimitro Sinicky (also spelled Sinizki) was a Canadian soldier executed by firing squad for cowardice during World War I on 9 October 1917. Born in Kiev, Russian Empire (modern-day Ukraine), he migrated to Canada before the war and enlisted in Winnipeg, Manitoba. He holds the sombre distinction of being the only soldier in the Canadian Expeditionary Force (CEF) to be shot at dawn specifically for the military offense of cowardice. While on active duty in Belgium, Sinicky refused orders to put on his equipment and move to the front lines. The following night, while being marched to the front under an armed escort, he sat down and refused to move any further. During his court-martial, Sinicky stated that he disobeyed orders because he "was afraid and feared being wounded." His explanation was rejected under the strict military laws of the era. He was executed at dawn

Private Charles Skilton avoided disciplinary action, due to a lack of evidence. As the fighting on the Somme drew to a close 2 Division was still in action. During the last week in October the Fusiliers’ diary recorded just how bad the conditions could be. A week of heavy rain had turned the ground into mud. In the middle of November the battalion attacked the Quadrilateral, but reluctant soldier Private Skilton had gone absent in the interim.
